[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9e/1986_Jeno%27s_Pizza_-_15_-_Willie_Davis_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1986_Jeno's_Pizza_-_15_-_Willie_Davis_(cropped).jpg)

The [Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") defeated the [Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") in the first [AFL–NFL World Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_World_Championship_Game "AFL–NFL World Championship Game") ([Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")).

The [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") is the annual [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") game that determines the champion of the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL). The game culminates a [season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_regular_season "National Football League regular season") that begins in the previous calendar year, and is the conclusion of the [NFL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_playoffs "National Football League playoffs"). The winner receives the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy"). The contest is held in an American city, chosen three to four years beforehand,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-1) usually at warm-weather sites or [domed stadiums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium#Types "Stadium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-2) Since January 1971, the winner of the [American Football Conference (AFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Championship_Game "AFC Championship Game") has faced the winner of the [National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_Championship_Game "NFC Championship Game") in the culmination of the NFL playoffs.

Before the [1970 merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_merger "AFL–NFL merger") between the [American Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League "American Football League") (AFL) and the NFL, the two leagues met in four such contests. The first two were marketed as the "AFL–NFL World Championship Game", but were also casually referred to as "the Super Bowl game" during the television broadcast.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-3)[Super Bowl III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_III "Super Bowl III") in January 1969 was the first such game that carried the "Super Bowl" moniker in official marketing; the names "[Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")" and "[Super Bowl II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II")" were retroactively applied to the first two games.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-nflaflwcg-4)

A total of 20 franchises, including teams that have relocated to another city or changed their name, have won the Super Bowl.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-record-5) There are four [NFL teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_team "NFL team") that have never appeared in a Super Bowl: the [Cleveland Browns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns"), [Detroit Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Lions "Detroit Lions"), [Jacksonville Jaguars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Jaguars "Jacksonville Jaguars"), and [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans"), though both the Browns ([1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_NFL_Championship_Game "1950 NFL Championship Game"), [1954](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_NFL_Championship_Game "1954 NFL Championship Game"), [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_NFL_Championship_Game "1955 NFL Championship Game"), [1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_NFL_Championship_Game "1964 NFL Championship Game")) and Lions ([1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_NFL_Championship_Game "1935 NFL Championship Game"), [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_NFL_Championship_Game "1952 NFL Championship Game"), [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_NFL_Championship_Game "1953 NFL Championship Game"), [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_NFL_Championship_Game "1957 NFL Championship Game")) had won [NFL Championship Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Championship_Game "NFL Championship Game") prior to the creation of the Super Bowl in the [1966 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NFL_season "1966 NFL season").

The [1972 Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Miami_Dolphins_season "1972 Miami Dolphins season") capped off the only [perfect season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_season "Perfect season") in [NFL history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_National_Football_League "History of the National Football League") with their victory in [Super Bowl VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"). Only two franchises have ever won the Super Bowl while hosting at their home stadiums: the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") in [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") and the [Los Angeles Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl LVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVI "Super Bowl LVI"). The reigning champions are the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") following their victory over the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") in [Super Bowl LX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX "Super Bowl LX").

The [Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") defeated the [Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV") to win an unprecedented four championships in six years.

Eight franchises have won consecutive Super Bowls, one of which (Pittsburgh) has accomplished it twice:

*   [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") (Super Bowls [I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I") and [II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II"))
*   [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Dolphins "Miami Dolphins") ([VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII") and [VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VIII "Super Bowl VIII"))
*   [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") (twice: [IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IX "Super Bowl IX") and [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_X "Super Bowl X"); [XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIII "Super Bowl XIII") and [XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV"))
*   [San Francisco 49ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_49ers "San Francisco 49ers") ([XXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIII "Super Bowl XXIII") and [XXIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIV "Super Bowl XXIV"))
*   [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") ([XXVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVII "Super Bowl XXVII") and [XXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVIII "Super Bowl XXVIII"))
*   [Denver Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Broncos "Denver Broncos") ([XXXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXII "Super Bowl XXXII") and [XXXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXIII "Super Bowl XXXIII"))[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-BroncosStreaks-94)
*   [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") ([XXXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXVIII "Super Bowl XXXVIII") and [XXXIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXIX "Super Bowl XXXIX"))
*   [Kansas City Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") ([LVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII "Super Bowl LVII") and [LVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVIII "Super Bowl LVIII"))

Although no franchise to date has won three Super Bowls in a row, several have had eras of sustained success, nearly accomplishing a [three-peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-peat "Three-peat"):

*   The [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") won the first two Super Bowls, and also won the [NFL Championship Game the preceding year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_NFL_Championship_Game "1965 NFL Championship Game"). If the Super Bowl had been instituted that year, the Packers would have qualified and faced the Buffalo Bills of the AFL.
*   The [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Dolphins "Miami Dolphins") appeared in three consecutive Super Bowls ([VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VI "Super Bowl VI"), [VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"), and [VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VIII "Super Bowl VIII"))– winning the last two.
*   The [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") won two consecutive Super Bowls ([IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IX "Super Bowl IX") and [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_X "Super Bowl X")); they also won two more consecutive Super Bowls ([XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIII "Super Bowl XIII") and [XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV")) for four titles in six seasons.
*   The [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") won two consecutive Super Bowls ([XXVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVII "Super Bowl XXVII") and [XXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVIII "Super Bowl XXVIII")); the [Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Dallas_Cowboys_season "1995 Dallas Cowboys season") won [Super Bowl XXX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXX "Super Bowl XXX") the following year for three titles in four seasons.
*   The [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") won Super Bowls [XLIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLIX "Super Bowl XLIX"), [LI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LI "Super Bowl LI"), and [LIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIII "Super Bowl LIII") for three titles in five seasons. They also appeared in and lost [Super Bowl LII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LII "Super Bowl LII") to the [Philadelphia Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Philadelphia_Eagles_season "2017 Philadelphia Eagles season") following the 2017 season, giving them four Super Bowl appearances in five years.
*   The [Kansas City Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") came the closest to a three-peat, winning back-to-back Super Bowls in [LVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII "Super Bowl LVII") and [LVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVIII "Super Bowl LVIII") but losing their third consecutive appearance in [LIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIX "Super Bowl LIX"). They additionally won [LIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIV "Super Bowl LIV") several years beforehand, and lost [LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV"), for a total of five Super Bowl appearances in six seasons.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9e/1986_Jeno%27s_Pizza_-_15_-_Willie_Davis_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1986_Jeno's_Pizza_-_15_-_Willie_Davis_(cropped).jpg)

The [Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") defeated the [Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") in the first [AFL–NFL World Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_World_Championship_Game "AFL–NFL World Championship Game") ([Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")).

The [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") is the annual [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") game that determines the champion of the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL). The game culminates a [season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_regular_season "National Football League regular season") that begins in the previous calendar year, and is the conclusion of the [NFL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_playoffs "National Football League playoffs"). The winner receives the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy"). The contest is held in an American city, chosen three to four years beforehand,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-1) usually at warm-weather sites or [domed stadiums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium#Types "Stadium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-2) Since January 1971, the winner of the [American Football Conference (AFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Championship_Game "AFC Championship Game") has faced the winner of the [National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_Championship_Game "NFC Championship Game") in the culmination of the NFL playoffs.

Before the [1970 merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_merger "AFL–NFL merger") between the [American Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League "American Football League") (AFL) and the NFL, the two leagues met in four such contests. The first two were marketed as the "AFL–NFL World Championship Game", but were also casually referred to as "the Super Bowl game" during the television broadcast.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-3)[Super Bowl III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_III "Super Bowl III") in January 1969 was the first such game that carried the "Super Bowl" moniker in official marketing; the names "[Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")" and "[Super Bowl II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II")" were retroactively applied to the first two games.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-nflaflwcg-4)

A total of 20 franchises, including teams that have relocated to another city or changed their name, have won the Super Bowl.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-record-5) There are four [NFL teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_team "NFL team") that have never appeared in a Super Bowl: the [Cleveland Browns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns"), [Detroit Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Lions "Detroit Lions"), [Jacksonville Jaguars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Jaguars "Jacksonville Jaguars"), and [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans"), though both the Browns ([1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_NFL_Championship_Game "1950 NFL Championship Game"), [1954](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_NFL_Championship_Game "1954 NFL Championship Game"), [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_NFL_Championship_Game "1955 NFL Championship Game"), [1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_NFL_Championship_Game "1964 NFL Championship Game")) and Lions ([1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_NFL_Championship_Game "1935 NFL Championship Game"), [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_NFL_Championship_Game "1952 NFL Championship Game"), [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_NFL_Championship_Game "1953 NFL Championship Game"), [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_NFL_Championship_Game "1957 NFL Championship Game")) had won [NFL Championship Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Championship_Game "NFL Championship Game") prior to the creation of the Super Bowl in the [1966 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NFL_season "1966 NFL season").

The [1972 Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Miami_Dolphins_season "1972 Miami Dolphins season") capped off the only [perfect season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_season "Perfect season") in [NFL history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_National_Football_League "History of the National Football League") with their victory in [Super Bowl VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"). Only two franchises have ever won the Super Bowl while hosting at their home stadiums: the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") in [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") and the [Los Angeles Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl LVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVI "Super Bowl LVI"). The reigning champions are the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") following their victory over the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") in [Super Bowl LX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX "Super Bowl LX").

The 2022 NFL draft was the National Football League's 87th annual draft and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the Caesars Forum on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise next to Las Vegas. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the Las Vegas metropolitan area and the state of Nevada.

The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in 1991. Along with the 1972 and 2000 drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five Georgia defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since 2013. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since 1997, and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since 2014.

A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.[1]

Host cityedit

Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the 2020 NFL draft, coinciding with the Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic the draft was held as a virtual event. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.[2]

Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating red carpet on the man-made lake in front of the Bellagio and its fountains. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.[3][4]

Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event.[3][4] The Linq Promenade hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities.[3][4] Parts of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.[5]

Resolution JC-2A selectionsedit

Resolution JC-2A, enacted by the NFL in November 2020, rewards teams for developing minority candidates for head coach and/or general manager positions.[16] The resolution rewards teams whose minority candidates are hired away for one of those positions by awarding draft selections, which are at the end of the third round, after standard compensatory selections; if multiple teams qualify, they are awarded by draft order in the first round. These picks are in addition to, and have no impact on, the standard 32 compensatory selections.[17] Seven picks were awarded for the 2022 draft pursuant to the resolution.

 Cleveland received a third-round selection (99th overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Minnesota hiring vice president of football operations Kwesi Adofo-Mensah as general manager.[6]
 Baltimore received a third-round selection (100th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Houston hiring assistant head coach and passing game coordinator David Culley as head coach.[7]
 New Orleans received a third-round selection (101st overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Atlanta hiring pro scouting director Terry Fontenot as general manager.[8]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (102nd overall), a 2021 third-round selection and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for the NY Jets hiring defensive coordinator Robert Saleh as head coach and Washington hiring vice president of player personnel Martin Mayhew as general manager.[9][10][11]
 Kansas City received a third-round selection (103rd overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Chicago hiring executive director of player personnel Ryan Poles as general manager.[12]
 The LA Rams received a third-round selection (104th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Detroit hiring college scouting director Brad Holmes as general manager.[13]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (105th overall) and another 2023 third-round selection when Miami hired offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as head coach.[14]
Notesedit
 Players are identified as Pro Bowlers if they were selected for the Pro Bowl at any time in their career.

Forfeited selections

 New Orleans forfeited a sixth-round selection as a penalty for repeated violations of the league's COVID-19 guidelines.[15]

The 2022 NFL draft was the National Football League's 87th annual draft and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the Caesars Forum on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise next to Las Vegas. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the Las Vegas metropolitan area and the state of Nevada.

The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in 1991. Along with the 1972 and 2000 drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five Georgia defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since 2013. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since 1997, and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since 2014.

A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.[1]

Host cityedit

Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the 2020 NFL draft, coinciding with the Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic the draft was held as a virtual event. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.[2]

Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating red carpet on the man-made lake in front of the Bellagio and its fountains. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.[3][4]

Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event.[3][4] The Linq Promenade hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities.[3][4] Parts of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.[5]

(PD) indicates trades completed prior to the start of the draft (i.e. Pre-Draft), while (D) denotes trades which took place during the 2022 draft.

Round 1

 No. 7: Chicago → NY Giants (PD). Chicago traded first- and fourth-round selections (7th and 112th overall), and 2021 first- and fourth-round selections to the NY Giants in exchange for a 2021 first-round selection.[trade 1]
 No. 9: Denver → Seattle (PD). Denver traded first-, second- and fifth-round selections (9th, 40th and 145th overall), 2023 first- and second-round selections, QB Drew Lock, TE Noah Fant and DT Shelby Harris to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a fourth-round selection (116th overall) and QB Russell Wilson.[trade 2]
 No. 10: Seattle → NY Jets (PD). Seattle traded a first-round selection (10th overall), 2021 first- and third-round selections, and S Bradley McDougald to the NY Jets in exchange for a fourth-round selection (109th overall) and S Jamal Adams.[trade 3]
 No. 11: Washington → New Orleans (D). Washington traded a first-round selection (11th overall) to New Orleans in exchange for first-, third- and fourth-round selections (16th, 98th and 120th overall).[trade 4]
 No. 12: Minnesota → Detroit (D). Minnesota traded first- and second-round selections (12th and 46th overall) to the Detroit Lions in exchange for first-, second- and third-round selections (32nd, 34th and 66th overall).[trade 4]
 No. 13: Cleveland → Houston → Philadelphia. Multiple trades:
       Cleveland → Houston (PD). Cleveland traded first- and fourth-round selections (13th and 107th overall), 2023 first- and third-round selections, and 2024 first- and fourth-round selections to Houston in exchange for a 2024 sixth-round selection and QB Deshaun Watson.[trade 5]

 No. 15: Miami → Philadelphia → Houston. Multiple trades:
       Miami → Philadelphia (PD). Miami traded a first-round selection (15th overall), and 2021 first- and fourth-round selections to Philadelphia in exchange for 2021 first- and fifth-round selections.[trade 6]
       Philadelphia → Houston (D). See Round 1: Houston → Philadelphia.[trade 4]
 No. 16: Indianapolis → Philadelphia → New Orleans → Washington. Multiple trades:
       Indianapolis → Philadelphia (PD). Indianapolis traded a conditional first-round selection (16th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection to Philadelphia in exchange for QB Carson Wentz. The conditional selection was upgraded from the second round because Wentz played 75% of Indianapolis' offensive snaps.[trade 7]
       Philadelphia → New Orleans (PD). Philadelphia traded two first-round selections and a sixth-round selection (16th, 19th and 194th overall) to New Orleans in exchange for first-, third- and seventh-round selections (18th, 101st and 237th overall), a 2023 first-round selection and a 2024 second-round selection.[trade 8]

Resolution JC-2A selectionsedit

Resolution JC-2A, enacted by the NFL in November 2020, rewards teams for developing minority candidates for head coach and/or general manager positions.[16] The resolution rewards teams whose minority candidates are hired away for one of those positions by awarding draft selections, which are at the end of the third round, after standard compensatory selections; if multiple teams qualify, they are awarded by draft order in the first round. These picks are in addition to, and have no impact on, the standard 32 compensatory selections.[17] Seven picks were awarded for the 2022 draft pursuant to the resolution.

 Cleveland received a third-round selection (99th overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Minnesota hiring vice president of football operations Kwesi Adofo-Mensah as general manager.[6]
 Baltimore received a third-round selection (100th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Houston hiring assistant head coach and passing game coordinator David Culley as head coach.[7]
 New Orleans received a third-round selection (101st overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Atlanta hiring pro scouting director Terry Fontenot as general manager.[8]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (102nd overall), a 2021 third-round selection and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for the NY Jets hiring defensive coordinator Robert Saleh as head coach and Washington hiring vice president of player personnel Martin Mayhew as general manager.[9][10][11]
 Kansas City received a third-round selection (103rd overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Chicago hiring executive director of player personnel Ryan Poles as general manager.[12]
 The LA Rams received a third-round selection (104th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Detroit hiring college scouting director Brad Holmes as general manager.[13]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (105th overall) and another 2023 third-round selection when Miami hired offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as head coach.[14]
Notesedit
 Players are identified as Pro Bowlers if they were selected for the Pro Bowl at any time in their career.

Forfeited selections

 New Orleans forfeited a sixth-round selection as a penalty for repeated violations of the league's COVID-19 guidelines.[15]

# 2022 NFL Draft picks by college team, school: Georgia defense sets first-round record, SEC dominates again

## Georgia and the SEC led the way among the schools and conferences represented Thursday night

[![Image 192: David Cobb ](https://sportshub.cbsistatic.com/i/r/2020/01/27/927cdfbb-c58c-42f7-b2cd-b6028d112ebe/thumbnail/80x80/20c71c6e361e25a5a509826e42528def/david-cobb.png)](https://www.cbssports.com/writers/david-cobb/)

Georgia made history in the first round of the 2022 NFL Draft on Thursday night when the Bulldogs had five defensive players from their national championship team selected in the first round. It marks the first time a college team has seen that many players from its defensive unit taken among the top 32 picks in a draft.

Consider that no other entire program had more than two players selected in Round 1, and Georgia's achievement is even more impressive. In fact, the Dawgs had more defenders selected than the ACC, Pac-12, AAC respectively had total picks.

Highlighting UGA's haul on Thursday was No. 1 overall pick Travon Walker, a defensive end who went to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Following Walker's selection, a bit of collegiate diversity ensued as five of the first six picks came from different conferences. But by night's end, the opening round featured a familiar flavor as 12 of the 32 picks came from SEC schools.

Georgia led the way its five overall selections: No. 13 pick Jordan Davis (Eagles), No. 22 pick Quay Walker (Packers) and No. 28 pick Devonte Wyatt (Packers) and No. 32 pick Lewis Cine (Vikings) joined Travon Walker in the festivities. All five played key roles in helping Georgia win a national title this past season, and they likely won't be the last defensive players selected from an all-time great Georgia defense as the draft continues Friday and Saturday. In fact, many were surprised Nakobe Dean was not among the first 32 picks, but he should be off the board early in Round 2.

The SEC once again led the way with 12 first-round picks, the same number of players it had chosen last year. In fact, the Big Ten also repeated its second-place finish with seven first-round picks, again mirroring its number of selections from a year ago. The Big Ten's haul was headlined by No. 2 pick Aiden Hutchinson, a defensive end from Michigan.

From a collegiate perspective, there was another bit of history on Thursday night. Alabama [tied Miami's record](https://www.cbssports.com/college-football/news/2022-nfl-draft-alabama-ties-miami-for-college-football-record-with-first-rounder-in-14th-straight-draft/) of 14 straight drafts with at least one first-round selection as offensive lineman Evan Neal (No. 7 to the Giants) and receiver Jameson Williams (No. 12 to the Lions) each went in the first round. The Crimson Tide are on pace to break that record in 2023.

Here's 2022 NFL Draft broken down by school at the conclusion of the first round.

Georgia made history in the first round of the 2022 NFL Draft on Thursday night when the Bulldogs had five defensive players from their national championship team selected in the first round. It marks the first time a college team has seen that many players from its defensive unit taken among the top 32 picks in a draft.

Consider that no other entire program had more than two players selected in Round 1, and Georgia's achievement is even more impressive. In fact, the Dawgs had more defenders selected than the ACC, Pac-12, AAC respectively had total picks.

Highlighting UGA's haul on Thursday was No. 1 overall pick Travon Walker, a defensive end who went to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Following Walker's selection, a bit of collegiate diversity ensued as five of the first six picks came from different conferences. But by night's end, the opening round featured a familiar flavor as 12 of the 32 picks came from SEC schools.

Georgia led the way its five overall selections: No. 13 pick Jordan Davis (Eagles), No. 22 pick Quay Walker (Packers) and No. 28 pick Devonte Wyatt (Packers) and No. 32 pick Lewis Cine (Vikings) joined Travon Walker in the festivities. All five played key roles in helping Georgia win a national title this past season, and they likely won't be the last defensive players selected from an all-time great Georgia defense as the draft continues Friday and Saturday. In fact, many were surprised Nakobe Dean was not among the first 32 picks, but he should be off the board early in Round 2.

The SEC once again led the way with 12 first-round picks, the same number of players it had chosen last year. In fact, the Big Ten also repeated its second-place finish with seven first-round picks, again mirroring its number of selections from a year ago. The Big Ten's haul was headlined by No. 2 pick Aiden Hutchinson, a defensive end from Michigan.

From a collegiate perspective, there was another bit of history on Thursday night. Alabama [tied Miami's record](https://www.cbssports.com/college-football/news/2022-nfl-draft-alabama-ties-miami-for-college-football-record-with-first-rounder-in-14th-straight-draft/) of 14 straight drafts with at least one first-round selection as offensive lineman Evan Neal (No. 7 to the Giants) and receiver Jameson Williams (No. 12 to the Lions) each went in the first round. The Crimson Tide are on pace to break that record in 2023.

The [2022 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NFL_season "2022 NFL season") was the [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers")' 90th in the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL) and their 16th under [head coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pittsburgh_Steelers_head_coaches "List of Pittsburgh Steelers head coaches")[Mike Tomlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Tomlin "Mike Tomlin").

This was their first season since [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2003 Pittsburgh Steelers season") without long-time quarterback [Ben Roethlisberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Roethlisberger "Ben Roethlisberger") on the roster, as he announced his retirement on January 27, 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-1) It was also the first season since [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "1999 Pittsburgh Steelers season") without long-time general manager [Kevin Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Colbert "Kevin Colbert"), as he announced on January 28, 2022 that after 22 years with the organization, he would step down following the 2022 NFL draft.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-2) He was succeeded by [Omar Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Khan_(American_football) "Omar Khan (American football)") as general manager and Andy Weidl as assistant general manager on May 25, 2022.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-3)

The Steelers began their season with a 2–6 record, their worst start since [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2013 Pittsburgh Steelers season"), and failed to improve on their 9–7–1 record from 2021. Despite the initial setback, the Steelers would have a mid-season turnaround and stay in the playoff hunt through Week 18 and finished with a 9–8 record. However, they narrowly missed the playoffs—the Steelers tied with the [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Miami_Dolphins_season "2022 Miami Dolphins season") for the last Wild Card spot, but lost the tiebreaker based on the teams' Week 7 head-to-head meeting, won by the Dolphins. They maintained their streak of 19 consecutive non-losing seasons.

In an oddity, the 2022 Steelers played all 17 of their games in the Eastern time zone.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-4) The Steelers also traveled by far the fewest miles (6512 miles) of any team in the league in 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-5)

The Steelers started the 2022 season against the division rival Bengals in Cincinnati. The Steelers scored first in the first quarter when Minkah Fitzpatrick returned an interception 31 yards for a touchdown to make it 7–0. The Bengals made it 7–3 when Evan McPhearson made a 59-yard field goal. The Steelers then went ahead 10–3 after Chris Boswell kicked a 20-yard field goal. In the second quarter, the Steelers moved ahead 17–3 after Mitchell Trubisky found Najee Harris on a 1-yard touchdown pass. The Bengals drew closer at halftime when McPhearson made a 26-yard field goal to make it 17–6. After the break, the Bengals came within 3 in the third quarter when Joe Burrow found Tyler Boyd on a 2-yard touchdown pass (with a successful 2-point conversion) to make it 17–14. In the fourth quarter, the Steelers moved ahead by 6 when Boswell kicked a 48-yard field goal to make it 20–14. Later on in the quarter, the Bengals tied the game when Burrow found Ja'Marr Chase on a 6-yard touchdown pass (with a blocked PAT) to send the game into overtime tied at 20–20. After going back and forth on possessions, the Steelers managed to win the game when Boswell kicked the game winning 53-yard field goal with seconds left to make the final score 23–20.

With their 3-game losing streak against the Bengals snapped, the Steelers started their season 1–0. Over the course of the game, the Steelers forced 5 turnovers.

The Steelers traveled to Philadelphia to take on the Eagles. In the first quarter, the Eagles scored first when Jalen Hurts found A. J. Brown on a 39-yard touchdown pass to make it 7–0. The Steelers tied it at 7–7 later on in the quarter when Derek Watt found Chase Claypool on a 1-yard touchdown pass. After coming off of their bye week, the Steelers returned home for a game against the Saints. The Steelers made it 7–0 in the first quarter when George Pickens ran for a 1-yard touchdown. They made it 10–0 in the second quarter when Matthew Wright kicked a 33-yard field goal. The Saints were able to tie the game up before halftime at 10–10 when Wil Lutz kicked a 44-yard field goal, followed up by Andy Dalton and Juwan Johnson hooking up on a 15-yard touchdown pass. After a tough home win, the Steelers stayed at home for Round 2 against the Bengals. In the first quarter, the Bengals scored first when Evan McPherson kicked a 45-yard field goal to make it 3–0. The Steelers then tied it up when Matthew Wright kicked a 42-yard field goal to make it 3–3. The Bengals then moved back into the lead when Joe Burrow found Samaje Berine on a 29-yard touchdown pass to make it 10–3. In the second quarter, the Steelers tied the game up at 10–10 when Najee Harris ran for a 19-yard touchdown. The Bengals then moved into the lead again when Burrow and Berine connected on a 11-yard touchdown pass to make it 17–10. The Steelers were able to tie it up at 17–17 when Kenny Pickett found George Pickens on a 24-yard touchdown pass. They took the lead at halftime 20–17 when Wright kicked a 30-yard field goal. In the third quarter, the Bengals retook the lead when Burrow found Trent Irwin on a 1-yard touchdown pass to make it 24–20. The Steelers drew closer when Wright kicked a 34-yard field goal to make it 24–23. The Bengals then pulled away when McPherson kicked a 54-yard field goal to make it 27–23. In the fourth quarter, the Bengals scored a couple more times: Burrow and Berine connected for a third time on a 6-yard touchdown pass for a 34–23 lead and then McPherson kicked a 44-yard field goal to make it 37–23. The Steelers concluded the scoring of the game when Harris ran for a 1-yard touchdown to make the final score 37–30.

With the loss, the Steelers fell to 3–7. It would be the team's worst 10-game start since [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2003 Pittsburgh Steelers season") and in turn the worst 10-game start under head coach Mike Tomlin.

After a win on Monday Night Football, the Steelers traveled south to face the Falcons. The Steelers scored the first quarter's only points when Matthew Wright kicked a 46-yard field goal to make it 3–0. They made it 6–0 in the second quarter when Wright kicked another 46-yard field goal. The Falcons got on the board when Younghoe Koo kicked a 51-yard field goal to make it 6–3. The Steelers moved ahead by double digits when Kenny Pickett found Connor Heyward on a 17-yard touchdown pass to make it 13–3. The Falcons came closer when Koo kicked a 51-yard field goal to make it 13–6. The Steelers moved ahead by double digits at halftime when Wright kicked a 48-yard field goal to make it 16–6. After the break, the Steelers went right back to work when Wright kicked a 33-yard field goal to make it 19–6. The Falcons shortened the lead later on in the quarter when Marcus Mariota found MyCole Pruitt on a 7-yard touchdown pass to make it 19–13. In the fourth, they would score the only points when Koo kicked a 28-yard field goal to make it 19–16. Getting the ball back with less than a minute left, the Falcons tried to rally. But Mariota threw the game-losing interception, sealing another Steelers victory.

With the win, the Steelers improved to 5–7.

The [2022 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NFL_season "2022 NFL season") was the [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers")' 90th in the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL) and their 16th under [head coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pittsburgh_Steelers_head_coaches "List of Pittsburgh Steelers head coaches")[Mike Tomlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Tomlin "Mike Tomlin").

This was their first season since [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2003 Pittsburgh Steelers season") without long-time quarterback [Ben Roethlisberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Roethlisberger "Ben Roethlisberger") on the roster, as he announced his retirement on January 27, 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-1) It was also the first season since [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "1999 Pittsburgh Steelers season") without long-time general manager [Kevin Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Colbert "Kevin Colbert"), as he announced on January 28, 2022 that after 22 years with the organization, he would step down following the 2022 NFL draft.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-2) He was succeeded by [Omar Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Khan_(American_football) "Omar Khan (American football)") as general manager and Andy Weidl as assistant general manager on May 25, 2022.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-3)

The Steelers began their season with a 2–6 record, their worst start since [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2013 Pittsburgh Steelers season"), and failed to improve on their 9–7–1 record from 2021. Despite the initial setback, the Steelers would have a mid-season turnaround and stay in the playoff hunt through Week 18 and finished with a 9–8 record. However, they narrowly missed the playoffs—the Steelers tied with the [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Miami_Dolphins_season "2022 Miami Dolphins season") for the last Wild Card spot, but lost the tiebreaker based on the teams' Week 7 head-to-head meeting, won by the Dolphins. They maintained their streak of 19 consecutive non-losing seasons.

In an oddity, the 2022 Steelers played all 17 of their games in the Eastern time zone.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-4) The Steelers also traveled by far the fewest miles (6512 miles) of any team in the league in 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season#cite_note-5)

The Steelers started the 2022 season against the division rival Bengals in Cincinnati. The Steelers scored first in the first quarter when Minkah Fitzpatrick returned an interception 31 yards for a touchdown to make it 7–0. The Bengals made it 7–3 when Evan McPhearson made a 59-yard field goal. The Steelers then went ahead 10–3 after Chris Boswell kicked a 20-yard field goal. In the second quarter, the Steelers moved ahead 17–3 after Mitchell Trubisky found Najee Harris on a 1-yard touchdown pass. The Bengals drew closer at halftime when McPhearson made a 26-yard field goal to make it 17–6. After the break, the Bengals came within 3 in the third quarter when Joe Burrow found Tyler Boyd on a 2-yard touchdown pass (with a successful 2-point conversion) to make it 17–14. In the fourth quarter, the Steelers moved ahead by 6 when Boswell kicked a 48-yard field goal to make it 20–14. Later on in the quarter, the Bengals tied the game when Burrow found Ja'Marr Chase on a 6-yard touchdown pass (with a blocked PAT) to send the game into overtime tied at 20–20. After going back and forth on possessions, the Steelers managed to win the game when Boswell kicked the game winning 53-yard field goal with seconds left to make the final score 23–20.

With their 3-game losing streak against the Bengals snapped, the Steelers started their season 1–0. Over the course of the game, the Steelers forced 5 turnovers.

After a tough win in Week 1, the Steelers went home for their opener against the Patriots. The Patriots scored first as Nick Folk kicked a 28-yard field goal 3–0 for the only score of the period. The Steelers tied it up in the second quarter when Chris Boswell kicked a 36-yard field goal to make it 3–3. The Patriots then took the lead when Mac Jones found Nelson Agholor on a 44-yard touchdown pass to make it 10–3 at halftime. In the third quarter, the Steelers came within 4 when Boswell kicked a 52-yard field goal to make it 10–6. Though, the Patriots would move ahead by double digits later on when Damien Harris ran for a 2-yard touchdown to make it 17–6. The Steelers were able to come within 3 after Mitchell Trubisky found Pat Freiermuth on an 8-yard touchdown pass (with a successful 2-point conversion) to make it 17–14. In the first quarter, the Steelers scored first when Najee Harris caught a 6-yard touchdown pass from Kenny Pickett to make the lead 7–0. After a tough home win, the Steelers stayed at home for Round 2 against the Bengals. In the first quarter, the Bengals scored first when Evan McPherson kicked a 45-yard field goal to make it 3–0. The Steelers then tied it up when Matthew Wright kicked a 42-yard field goal to make it 3–3. The Bengals then moved back into the lead when Joe Burrow found Samaje Berine on a 29-yard touchdown pass to make it 10–3. In the second quarter, the Steelers tied the game up at 10–10 when Najee Harris ran for a 19-yard touchdown. The Bengals then moved into the lead again when Burrow and Berine connected on a 11-yard touchdown pass to make it 17–10. The Steelers were able to tie it up at 17–17 when Kenny Pickett found George Pickens on a 24-yard touchdown pass. They took the lead at halftime 20–17 when Wright kicked a 30-yard field goal. In the third quarter, the Bengals retook the lead when Burrow found Trent Irwin on a 1-yard touchdown pass to make it 24–20. The Steelers drew closer when Wright kicked a 34-yard field goal to make it 24–23. The Bengals then pulled away when McPherson kicked a 54-yard field goal to make it 27–23. In the fourth quarter, the Bengals scored a couple more times: Burrow and Berine connected for a third time on a 6-yard touchdown pass for a 34–23 lead and then McPherson kicked a 44-yard field goal to make it 37–23. The Steelers concluded the scoring of the game when Harris ran for a 1-yard touchdown to make the final score 37–30.

With the loss, the Steelers fell to 3–7. It would be the team's worst 10-game start since [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2003 Pittsburgh Steelers season") and in turn the worst 10-game start under head coach Mike Tomlin.

After a tough loss at home, the Steelers traveled for a game against the Colts on Monday Night Football. The Steelers were able to make a 13–0 lead well into the first 2 quarters by way of Matthew Wright's 45 and 52 yard field goals and then a 6-yard touchdown run by Najee Harris. The Colts were able to get on the board in the second when Chase McLaughlin kicked a 51-yard field goal to make it 13–3. The Steelers pulled away as Wright closed the scoring of the first half with another field goal from 25 yards out to make it 16–3 at halftime. In the third quarter, it was all Colts as they found the end zone twice and were able to take a 17–16 lead: Johnathan Taylor's 2-yard run followed up by a 6-yard pass from Matt Ryan to Michael Pittman Jr. The Steelers responded in the fourth quarter by taking the lead back when Benny Snell ran for a 2-yard touchdown pass (with a successful 2-point conversion) to make the final score 24–17.

With the win, the Steelers improved to 4–7.

After a win on Monday Night Football, the Steelers traveled south to face the Falcons. The Steelers scored the first quarter's only points when Matthew Wright kicked a 46-yard field goal to make it 3–0. They made it 6–0 in the second quarter when Wright kicked another 46-yard field goal. The Falcons got on the board when Younghoe Koo kicked a 51-yard field goal to make it 6–3. The Steelers moved ahead by double digits when Kenny Pickett found Connor Heyward on a 17-yard touchdown pass to make it 13–3. The Falcons came closer when Koo kicked a 51-yard field goal to make it 13–6. The Steelers moved ahead by double digits at halftime when Wright kicked a 48-yard field goal to make it 16–6. After the break, the Steelers went right back to work when Wright kicked a 33-yard field goal to make it 19–6. The Falcons shortened the lead later on in the quarter when Marcus Mariota found MyCole Pruitt on a 7-yard touchdown pass to make it 19–13. In the fourth, they would score the only points when Koo kicked a 28-yard field goal to make it 19–16. Getting the ball back with less than a minute left, the Falcons tried to rally. But Mariota threw the game-losing interception, sealing another Steelers victory.

With the win, the Steelers improved to 5–7.

The **Southeastern Conference** (**SEC**) is a collegiate [athletic conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NCAA_conferences "List of NCAA conferences") whose member institutions are located primarily in the [South Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Central_United_States "South Central United States") and [Southeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States"). Its 16 members include the [flagship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship_university "Flagship university") public universities of 12 states, 3 additional public [land-grant universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university"), and 1 private research university. The conference is headquartered in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). The SEC participates in the [National Collegiate Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA) [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") in sports competitions. In [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football"), it is part of the [Football Bowl Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Football_Bowl_Subdivision "NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision") (FBS), formerly known as Division I-A.

The SEC was established in 1932 by 13 members of the [Southern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Conference "Southern Conference"). Three charter members left by the late 1960s, but additions in 1990 and 2012 grew the conference to 14 member institutions. The conference expanded to 16 members with the addition of the [University of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma") and the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas "University of Texas") in 2024.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-OUUT-3)

In [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_SEC_Championship_Game "1992 SEC Championship Game"), the SEC was the first NCAA Division I conference to have a [championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game") for football and was one of the founding member conferences of the [Bowl Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowl_Championship_Series "Bowl Championship Series") (BCS). The conference sponsors team championships in nine men's sports and thirteen women's sports. The conference distributed $721.8 million to its 14 schools in 2022.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-4)

### Current members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Current members")]

The SEC consists of 16 member institutions located in the U.S. states of [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") and [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").

The SEC was formerly divided into East and West Divisions, although the divisional alignment was not strictly geographic, with Missouri in the East Division while being farther west than all West Division schools except Arkansas and Texas A&M, and Auburn in the West Division despite being located farther east than East Division schools Missouri and Vanderbilt.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-d154-5) These divisional groupings were applied only in football, men's basketball (prior to 2011–12), baseball, and women's soccer both for scheduling and standings purposes. In football, the winner of each division met in the [SEC Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game"). The SEC eliminated its divisional groupings when Oklahoma and Texas joined in 2024.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-SevenSports-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-SixSports-7)

### Former members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Former members")]

Three schools have left the SEC, all charter members:

*   [The University of the South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee:_The_University_of_the_South "Sewanee: The University of the South") ("Sewanee") developed an elite college football program around the turn of the 20th century, with some observers opining that the [1899 "Iron Tigers"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1899_Sewanee_Tigers_football_team "1899 Sewanee Tigers football team") were the most dominant squad in history.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-19) However, after helping to establish the SEC in the early 1930s, it became clear that the small private institution's athletic teams could no longer compete with those from large state universities. [Sewanee Tigers football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee_Tigers_football "Sewanee Tigers football") squads never won a conference game, going 0–36 in league play over eight seasons while enjoying much more success against non-conference foes from comparably-sized institutions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20) As such, Sewanee opted to leave the SEC after the 1940 season and transitioned its athletic programs to the lower divisions of intercollegiate play.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sewanee1-21) The school is currently a member of the [Southern Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Athletic_Association "Southern Athletic Association") (SAA).[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-D3-22)
*   [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets "Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets") left the SEC in 1964 due to controversy over the conference's regulation of [recruiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_recruiting "College recruiting") and [scholarships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarship "Athletic scholarship"). Georgia Tech athletic director and head football coach [Bobby Dodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Dodd "Bobby Dodd") had lobbied the league to establish rules prohibiting several practices, particularly the oversigning of players by Alabama coach [Bear Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Bryant "Bear Bryant") and others.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-23) When league members voted against tightening the rules, Dodd withdrew the Yellow Jackets from the SEC. The school played as an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_FBS_independent_schools "NCAA Division I FBS independent schools") for several years until 1978, when Georgia Tech joined the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference") (ACC).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20)
*   [Tulane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave "Tulane Green Wave") left the SEC in 1966. Although the school's athletic squads were competitive in the conference's early days, the private institution's programs struggled to compete against large state universities. This was particularly true in football, where the [Green Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_football "Tulane Green Wave football") were SEC champions in [1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Tulane_Green_Wave_football_team "1949 Tulane Green Wave football team") but never again posted a winning record in conference play. Tulane left the SEC in 1966 and subsequently considered dropping to lower levels of NCAA competition or ending its football program to focus on academics.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-24) However, the school has remained in Division I and is currently in the [American Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Conference_(NCAA) "American Conference (NCAA)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Founding")]

The SEC was established December 8 and 9, 1932, in Knoxville, Tennessee, at the Farragut Hotel, when the thirteen members of the large [Southern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Conference "Southern Conference") located west and south of the [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") left to form their own conference. Ten of the thirteen founding members have remained in the conference since its inception: the [University of Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Alabama "University of Alabama"), [Auburn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auburn_University "Auburn University"), the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida"), the [University of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Georgia "University of Georgia"), the [University of Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kentucky "University of Kentucky"), [Louisiana State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_State_University "Louisiana State University") ("LSU"), the [University of Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi "University of Mississippi") ("Ole Miss"), [Mississippi State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_University "Mississippi State University"), the [University of Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee "University of Tennessee"), and [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University "Vanderbilt University"). The SEC had no formal headquarters during its first eight years of existence, but in 1940, former [Governor of Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Mississippi "Governor of Mississippi")[Martin "Mike" Conner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_S._Conner "Martin S. Conner") was named the conference's first president, with the league establishing its first corporate headquarters on the 13th floor of the [Standard Life Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Life_Building_(Jackson,_Mississippi)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Standard Life Building (Jackson, Mississippi) (page does not exist)") in downtown [Jackson, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi "Jackson, Mississippi"). The SEC office remained there until 1948, when it moved to [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"), where it remains.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-27) The three founding members that have since left the conference are [Sewanee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee_Tigers_football "Sewanee Tigers football"), who left after the 1940 season to drop all athletic scholarships and become a [D-III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_III "NCAA Division III") Independent; [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football "Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football"), who left after the 1963 season and became a D-I Independent; and [Tulane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_football "Tulane Green Wave football"), who left after the 1965 season and became a D-I Independent.

In 1935, the SEC became the first conference to legalize [athletic scholarships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarships "Athletic scholarships").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-28)

### Racial integration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Racial integration")]

[![Image 58](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg/250px-GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg)

[Bobby Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Grier_(Pittsburgh_Panthers) "Bobby Grier (Pittsburgh Panthers)") playing against the [Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football_team "1955 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team") in 1955

White southerners committed to maintaining segregation created controversy preceding the [1956 Sugar Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Sugar_Bowl "1956 Sugar Bowl"), when the [Pitt Panthers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Pittsburgh_Panthers_football_team "1955 Pittsburgh Panthers football team"), with African-American fullback [Bobby Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Grier_(American_football_player) "Bobby Grier (American football player)") on the roster, met the [Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football_team "1955 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-fcflu-29) White southern segregationists created controversy by claiming that Grier should be barred from the game due to his race, and whether Georgia Tech should even play at all due to Georgia's [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Georgia "List of governors of Georgia")[Marvin Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Griffin "Marvin Griffin")'s opposition to racial integration.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Mul%C3%A9-30)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-31)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-32) After Griffin publicly sent a telegram to the state's Board of Regents requesting Georgia Tech not to engage in racially integrated events, Georgia Tech's president [Blake R. Van Leer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_R._Van_Leer "Blake R. Van Leer") rejected the request and threatened to resign. The game went on as planned.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-33)

The 1959 Mississippi State men's basketball team, led by all-American [Bailey Howell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey_Howell "Bailey Howell"), finished its season 24–1, winning the conference title. They did not participate in the NCAA tournament as school and state officials would not permit the team to play against Black players from northern schools. Four years later, in 1963, [Loyola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962%E2%80%9363_Loyola_Ramblers_men's_basketball_team "1962–63 Loyola Ramblers men's basketball team"), with four black starters, played Mississippi State in the "[Game of Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Change "Game of Change")".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-34)

It was not until 1966 that African Americans first participated in an SEC athletic contest, and the first black scholarship athletes did not play in the SEC until the 1967–68 school year.

The first African American to compete in the SEC was Stephen Martin, who [walked on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk-on_(sports) "Walk-on (sports)") to the [Tulane baseball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_baseball "Tulane Green Wave baseball") in that school's final SEC season of 1966.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-35) In August of that same year, Kentucky enrolled [Nate Northington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Northington "Nate Northington") and Greg Page on football scholarships,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36) and Vanderbilt enrolled Godfrey Dillard and [Perry Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_Wallace "Perry Wallace") on basketball scholarships.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Carey-37) At the time, the NCAA did not allow freshmen to compete on varsity teams, which meant that these pioneers could not play until 1967. Page died from complications of a spinal cord injury suffered during a football practice before ever playing a game,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36) while Dillard suffered a career-altering injury before getting a chance to play for Vanderbilt's varsity and transferred to [Eastern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Michigan_Eagles_men's_basketball "Eastern Michigan Eagles men's basketball").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Carey-37) The remaining two both played in the 1967–68 school year. Northington made his overall debut against [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Indiana_Hoosiers_football_team "1967 Indiana Hoosiers football team") on September 23, 1967[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-38)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-39) and his SEC debut against Ole Miss the following week on September 30 (the day after Page's death[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36)), while Wallace made his varsity debut later that year.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-40)

### 1990 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1990 expansion")]

Further information: [Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Conference "Southwest Conference")

In 1990, the SEC expanded from ten to twelve member universities with the addition of the [Arkansas Razorbacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Razorbacks "Arkansas Razorbacks") and the [South Carolina Gamecocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_Gamecocks "South Carolina Gamecocks"). The two new members began SEC competition with the 1991–1992 basketball season.

At the same time, the SEC organized competition for some sports into two divisions. The Western Division comprised six of the seven member schools in the [Central Time Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone"), while the Eastern Division comprised the five member schools in the [Eastern Time Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") plus Vanderbilt, which is in the Central Time Zone but was placed in the Eastern Division to preserve its rivalry with Tennessee. Initially, the divisional format was used in football, baseball, and men's basketball. The divisional format was dropped for men's basketball following the 2011–2012 season.

Following expansion, the SEC was the first conference to receive permission from the NCAA to sponsor an annual [football championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game") that did not count against NCAA limits on regular-season contests, featuring the winners of the conference's Eastern and Western divisions.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-about-41) The [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_SEC_Championship_Game "1992 SEC Championship Game") and [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_SEC_Championship_Game "1993 SEC Championship Game") championship games were held at [Legion Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_Field "Legion Field") in Birmingham, and all championship games from [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_SEC_Championship_Game "1994 SEC Championship Game") onward have been held in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta")—first at the [Georgia Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Dome "Georgia Dome") until its closure and demolition after the 2016 season, and since 2017 at [Mercedes-Benz Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_Stadium "Mercedes-Benz Stadium").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-about-41)

### 2012 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2012 expansion")]

See also: [2010–12 Southeastern Conference realignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9312_Southeastern_Conference_realignment "2010–12 Southeastern Conference realignment")

On September 25, 2011, the SEC Presidents and Chancellors, acting unanimously, announced that [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") would join the SEC effective July 1, 2012, to begin competition in nineteen of the twenty sports sponsored by the SEC during the 2012–13 academic year.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-42) On November 6, 2011, the SEC commissioner announced that the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri") would also join the SEC on July 1, 2012.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-43) For football, Texas A&M was scheduled to compete in the Western Division, and Missouri in the Eastern Division.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-washpo-secnewmember20111228-44)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-bhamnews28dec2011-45)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-espn-28dec2011-46)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-sportingnewsdecember282011-47) Texas A&M and Missouri both left the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference").

### 2024 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2024 expansion")]

See also: [2021–2026 NCAA conference realignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932026_NCAA_conference_realignment "2021–2026 NCAA conference realignment")

On July 27, 2021, [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma") and [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") formally notified the SEC they were seeking "an invitation for membership." In a joint letter, Texas president Jay Hartzell and Oklahoma president Joseph Harroz Jr. wrote, "We believe that there would be mutual benefit to the Universities on the one hand, and the SEC on the other hand, for the Universities to become members of the SEC."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-:0-48) On July 29, 2021, the presidents of the current 14 schools of the SEC voted unanimously to extend an offer of admission to Oklahoma and Texas.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-:1-49) The boards of regents for both institutions on July 30, 2021, accepted conference membership, and the schools were tentatively scheduled to join the league in 2025.

On February 9, 2023, the Big 12, Texas, and Oklahoma announced they had reached a buyout agreement that allowed the schools to join the SEC in 2024. The [Texas Longhorns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns "Texas Longhorns") and [Oklahoma Sooners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Sooners "Oklahoma Sooners") athletic teams thus began league play during the 2024–25 academic year.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-50)
