## SEC Academic Network

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: SEC Academic Network")]

In 2005, the member institutions of the Southeastern Conference formed the SEC Academic Consortium (SECAC), a collaborative endeavor designed to promote research, scholarship, and achievement amongst the universities.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-52)

In 2011, the SEC Academic Consortium relocated from its original home on the campus of the [University of Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arkansas "University of Arkansas") to the SEC headquarters in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama") and was renamed SECU. The SECU rebranded its mission to better serve as a means through which the collaborative academic endeavors and achievements of Southeastern Conference universities would be promoted and advanced. The SECU's goals included highlighting the endeavors and achievements of SEC [faculty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_(academic_staff) "Faculty (academic staff)"), students, and its universities; advancing the academic reputation of SEC universities; identifying and preparing future leaders for high-level service in academia; increasing the amount and type of [study abroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Study_abroad "Study abroad") opportunities available for students; and providing opportunities for collaboration among SEC university personnel.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-53)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-54) The [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference"), since 1958, has had a similar program, now called the [Big Ten Academic Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Academic_Alliance "Big Ten Academic Alliance").

The SEC Symposium component of SECU was crafted by [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University "Vanderbilt University") Chancellor [Nicholas S. Zeppos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_S._Zeppos "Nicholas S. Zeppos"), who at the time was the Vice President of the SEC Executive Committee and liaison to SECU.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-55) In an interview with Dr. Zeppos about the formation of the SECU he noted, "that the member institutions of the Southeastern Conference are committed to a shared mission of fostering research, scholarship, and achievement. The SEC Symposium represents a platform to connect, collaborate and promote a productive dialogue that will span disciplinary and institutional boundaries and allow us to work together for the betterment of society."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-56)

The SEC Academic Network was created in 2009 in partnership with [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN"). The SEC Academic Network was an online library of institutionally produced videos featuring academic initiatives and stories from all Southeastern Conference institutions. The SEC Academic Network was officially merged into the SECU operation.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-57)

Total expenses includes coach and staff salaries, scholarships, buildings and grounds, maintenance, utilities and rental fees, recruiting, team travel, equipment and uniforms, conference dues, and insurance.

The **Southeastern Conference** (**SEC**) is a collegiate [athletic conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NCAA_conferences "List of NCAA conferences") whose member institutions are located primarily in the [South Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Central_United_States "South Central United States") and [Southeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States"). Its 16 members include the [flagship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship_university "Flagship university") public universities of 12 states, 3 additional public [land-grant universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university"), and 1 private research university. The conference is headquartered in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). The SEC participates in the [National Collegiate Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA) [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") in sports competitions. In [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football"), it is part of the [Football Bowl Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Football_Bowl_Subdivision "NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision") (FBS), formerly known as Division I-A.

The SEC was established in 1932 by 13 members of the [Southern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Conference "Southern Conference"). Three charter members left by the late 1960s, but additions in 1990 and 2012 grew the conference to 14 member institutions. The conference expanded to 16 members with the addition of the [University of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma") and the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas "University of Texas") in 2024.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-OUUT-3)

In [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_SEC_Championship_Game "1992 SEC Championship Game"), the SEC was the first NCAA Division I conference to have a [championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game") for football and was one of the founding member conferences of the [Bowl Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowl_Championship_Series "Bowl Championship Series") (BCS). The conference sponsors team championships in nine men's sports and thirteen women's sports. The conference distributed $721.8 million to its 14 schools in 2022.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-4)

### Current members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Current members")]

The SEC consists of 16 member institutions located in the U.S. states of [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") and [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").

The SEC was formerly divided into East and West Divisions, although the divisional alignment was not strictly geographic, with Missouri in the East Division while being farther west than all West Division schools except Arkansas and Texas A&M, and Auburn in the West Division despite being located farther east than East Division schools Missouri and Vanderbilt.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-d154-5) These divisional groupings were applied only in football, men's basketball (prior to 2011–12), baseball, and women's soccer both for scheduling and standings purposes. In football, the winner of each division met in the [SEC Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game"). The SEC eliminated its divisional groupings when Oklahoma and Texas joined in 2024.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-SevenSports-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-SixSports-7)

### Former members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Former members")]

Three schools have left the SEC, all charter members:

*   [The University of the South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee:_The_University_of_the_South "Sewanee: The University of the South") ("Sewanee") developed an elite college football program around the turn of the 20th century, with some observers opining that the [1899 "Iron Tigers"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1899_Sewanee_Tigers_football_team "1899 Sewanee Tigers football team") were the most dominant squad in history.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-19) However, after helping to establish the SEC in the early 1930s, it became clear that the small private institution's athletic teams could no longer compete with those from large state universities. [Sewanee Tigers football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee_Tigers_football "Sewanee Tigers football") squads never won a conference game, going 0–36 in league play over eight seasons while enjoying much more success against non-conference foes from comparably-sized institutions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20) As such, Sewanee opted to leave the SEC after the 1940 season and transitioned its athletic programs to the lower divisions of intercollegiate play.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sewanee1-21) The school is currently a member of the [Southern Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Athletic_Association "Southern Athletic Association") (SAA).[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-D3-22)
*   [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets "Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets") left the SEC in 1964 due to controversy over the conference's regulation of [recruiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_recruiting "College recruiting") and [scholarships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarship "Athletic scholarship"). Georgia Tech athletic director and head football coach [Bobby Dodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Dodd "Bobby Dodd") had lobbied the league to establish rules prohibiting several practices, particularly the oversigning of players by Alabama coach [Bear Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Bryant "Bear Bryant") and others.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-23) When league members voted against tightening the rules, Dodd withdrew the Yellow Jackets from the SEC. The school played as an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_FBS_independent_schools "NCAA Division I FBS independent schools") for several years until 1978, when Georgia Tech joined the [Atlantic Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference "Atlantic Coast Conference") (ACC).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20)
*   [Tulane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave "Tulane Green Wave") left the SEC in 1966. Although the school's athletic squads were competitive in the conference's early days, the private institution's programs struggled to compete against large state universities. This was particularly true in football, where the [Green Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_football "Tulane Green Wave football") were SEC champions in [1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Tulane_Green_Wave_football_team "1949 Tulane Green Wave football team") but never again posted a winning record in conference play. Tulane left the SEC in 1966 and subsequently considered dropping to lower levels of NCAA competition or ending its football program to focus on academics.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-24) However, the school has remained in Division I and is currently in the [American Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Conference_(NCAA) "American Conference (NCAA)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-charter-20)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Founding")]

The SEC was established December 8 and 9, 1932, in Knoxville, Tennessee, at the Farragut Hotel, when the thirteen members of the large [Southern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Conference "Southern Conference") located west and south of the [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") left to form their own conference. Ten of the thirteen founding members have remained in the conference since its inception: the [University of Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Alabama "University of Alabama"), [Auburn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auburn_University "Auburn University"), the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida"), the [University of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Georgia "University of Georgia"), the [University of Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kentucky "University of Kentucky"), [Louisiana State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_State_University "Louisiana State University") ("LSU"), the [University of Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi "University of Mississippi") ("Ole Miss"), [Mississippi State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_University "Mississippi State University"), the [University of Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee "University of Tennessee"), and [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University "Vanderbilt University"). The SEC had no formal headquarters during its first eight years of existence, but in 1940, former [Governor of Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Mississippi "Governor of Mississippi")[Martin "Mike" Conner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_S._Conner "Martin S. Conner") was named the conference's first president, with the league establishing its first corporate headquarters on the 13th floor of the [Standard Life Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Life_Building_(Jackson,_Mississippi)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Standard Life Building (Jackson, Mississippi) (page does not exist)") in downtown [Jackson, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi "Jackson, Mississippi"). The SEC office remained there until 1948, when it moved to [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"), where it remains.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-27) The three founding members that have since left the conference are [Sewanee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee_Tigers_football "Sewanee Tigers football"), who left after the 1940 season to drop all athletic scholarships and become a [D-III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_III "NCAA Division III") Independent; [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football "Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football"), who left after the 1963 season and became a D-I Independent; and [Tulane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_football "Tulane Green Wave football"), who left after the 1965 season and became a D-I Independent.

In 1935, the SEC became the first conference to legalize [athletic scholarships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarships "Athletic scholarships").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-28)

### Racial integration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Racial integration")]

[![Image 58](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg/250px-GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GreirSugarBwolpg322_1956OWL.jpg)

[Bobby Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Grier_(Pittsburgh_Panthers) "Bobby Grier (Pittsburgh Panthers)") playing against the [Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football_team "1955 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team") in 1955

White southerners committed to maintaining segregation created controversy preceding the [1956 Sugar Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Sugar_Bowl "1956 Sugar Bowl"), when the [Pitt Panthers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Pittsburgh_Panthers_football_team "1955 Pittsburgh Panthers football team"), with African-American fullback [Bobby Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Grier_(American_football_player) "Bobby Grier (American football player)") on the roster, met the [Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football_team "1955 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-fcflu-29) White southern segregationists created controversy by claiming that Grier should be barred from the game due to his race, and whether Georgia Tech should even play at all due to Georgia's [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Georgia "List of governors of Georgia")[Marvin Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Griffin "Marvin Griffin")'s opposition to racial integration.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Mul%C3%A9-30)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-31)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-32) After Griffin publicly sent a telegram to the state's Board of Regents requesting Georgia Tech not to engage in racially integrated events, Georgia Tech's president [Blake R. Van Leer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_R._Van_Leer "Blake R. Van Leer") rejected the request and threatened to resign. The game went on as planned.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-33)

The 1959 Mississippi State men's basketball team, led by all-American [Bailey Howell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey_Howell "Bailey Howell"), finished its season 24–1, winning the conference title. They did not participate in the NCAA tournament as school and state officials would not permit the team to play against Black players from northern schools. Four years later, in 1963, [Loyola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962%E2%80%9363_Loyola_Ramblers_men's_basketball_team "1962–63 Loyola Ramblers men's basketball team"), with four black starters, played Mississippi State in the "[Game of Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Change "Game of Change")".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-34)

It was not until 1966 that African Americans first participated in an SEC athletic contest, and the first black scholarship athletes did not play in the SEC until the 1967–68 school year.

The first African American to compete in the SEC was Stephen Martin, who [walked on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk-on_(sports) "Walk-on (sports)") to the [Tulane baseball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_Green_Wave_baseball "Tulane Green Wave baseball") in that school's final SEC season of 1966.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-35) In August of that same year, Kentucky enrolled [Nate Northington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Northington "Nate Northington") and Greg Page on football scholarships,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36) and Vanderbilt enrolled Godfrey Dillard and [Perry Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_Wallace "Perry Wallace") on basketball scholarships.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Carey-37) At the time, the NCAA did not allow freshmen to compete on varsity teams, which meant that these pioneers could not play until 1967. Page died from complications of a spinal cord injury suffered during a football practice before ever playing a game,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36) while Dillard suffered a career-altering injury before getting a chance to play for Vanderbilt's varsity and transferred to [Eastern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Michigan_Eagles_men's_basketball "Eastern Michigan Eagles men's basketball").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Carey-37) The remaining two both played in the 1967–68 school year. Northington made his overall debut against [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Indiana_Hoosiers_football_team "1967 Indiana Hoosiers football team") on September 23, 1967[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-38)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-39) and his SEC debut against Ole Miss the following week on September 30 (the day after Page's death[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-Sculpture-36)), while Wallace made his varsity debut later that year.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-40)

### 1990 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1990 expansion")]

Further information: [Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Conference "Southwest Conference")

In 1990, the SEC expanded from ten to twelve member universities with the addition of the [Arkansas Razorbacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Razorbacks "Arkansas Razorbacks") and the [South Carolina Gamecocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_Gamecocks "South Carolina Gamecocks"). The two new members began SEC competition with the 1991–1992 basketball season.

At the same time, the SEC organized competition for some sports into two divisions. The Western Division comprised six of the seven member schools in the [Central Time Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone"), while the Eastern Division comprised the five member schools in the [Eastern Time Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") plus Vanderbilt, which is in the Central Time Zone but was placed in the Eastern Division to preserve its rivalry with Tennessee. Initially, the divisional format was used in football, baseball, and men's basketball. The divisional format was dropped for men's basketball following the 2011–2012 season.

Following expansion, the SEC was the first conference to receive permission from the NCAA to sponsor an annual [football championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEC_Championship_Game "SEC Championship Game") that did not count against NCAA limits on regular-season contests, featuring the winners of the conference's Eastern and Western divisions.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-about-41) The [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_SEC_Championship_Game "1992 SEC Championship Game") and [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_SEC_Championship_Game "1993 SEC Championship Game") championship games were held at [Legion Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_Field "Legion Field") in Birmingham, and all championship games from [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_SEC_Championship_Game "1994 SEC Championship Game") onward have been held in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta")—first at the [Georgia Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Dome "Georgia Dome") until its closure and demolition after the 2016 season, and since 2017 at [Mercedes-Benz Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_Stadium "Mercedes-Benz Stadium").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-about-41)

### 2012 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2012 expansion")]

See also: [2010–12 Southeastern Conference realignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9312_Southeastern_Conference_realignment "2010–12 Southeastern Conference realignment")

On September 25, 2011, the SEC Presidents and Chancellors, acting unanimously, announced that [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") would join the SEC effective July 1, 2012, to begin competition in nineteen of the twenty sports sponsored by the SEC during the 2012–13 academic year.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-42) On November 6, 2011, the SEC commissioner announced that the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri") would also join the SEC on July 1, 2012.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-43) For football, Texas A&M was scheduled to compete in the Western Division, and Missouri in the Eastern Division.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-washpo-secnewmember20111228-44)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-bhamnews28dec2011-45)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-espn-28dec2011-46)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-sportingnewsdecember282011-47) Texas A&M and Missouri both left the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference").

### 2024 expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2024 expansion")]

See also: [2021–2026 NCAA conference realignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932026_NCAA_conference_realignment "2021–2026 NCAA conference realignment")

On July 27, 2021, [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma") and [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") formally notified the SEC they were seeking "an invitation for membership." In a joint letter, Texas president Jay Hartzell and Oklahoma president Joseph Harroz Jr. wrote, "We believe that there would be mutual benefit to the Universities on the one hand, and the SEC on the other hand, for the Universities to become members of the SEC."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-:0-48) On July 29, 2021, the presidents of the current 14 schools of the SEC voted unanimously to extend an offer of admission to Oklahoma and Texas.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-:1-49) The boards of regents for both institutions on July 30, 2021, accepted conference membership, and the schools were tentatively scheduled to join the league in 2025.

On February 9, 2023, the Big 12, Texas, and Oklahoma announced they had reached a buyout agreement that allowed the schools to join the SEC in 2024. The [Texas Longhorns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Longhorns "Texas Longhorns") and [Oklahoma Sooners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Sooners "Oklahoma Sooners") athletic teams thus began league play during the 2024–25 academic year.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-50)

## SEC Academic Network

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southeastern_Conference&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: SEC Academic Network")]

In 2005, the member institutions of the Southeastern Conference formed the SEC Academic Consortium (SECAC), a collaborative endeavor designed to promote research, scholarship, and achievement amongst the universities.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-52)

In 2011, the SEC Academic Consortium relocated from its original home on the campus of the [University of Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arkansas "University of Arkansas") to the SEC headquarters in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama") and was renamed SECU. The SECU rebranded its mission to better serve as a means through which the collaborative academic endeavors and achievements of Southeastern Conference universities would be promoted and advanced. The SECU's goals included highlighting the endeavors and achievements of SEC [faculty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_(academic_staff) "Faculty (academic staff)"), students, and its universities; advancing the academic reputation of SEC universities; identifying and preparing future leaders for high-level service in academia; increasing the amount and type of [study abroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Study_abroad "Study abroad") opportunities available for students; and providing opportunities for collaboration among SEC university personnel.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-53)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-54) The [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference"), since 1958, has had a similar program, now called the [Big Ten Academic Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Academic_Alliance "Big Ten Academic Alliance").

The SEC Symposium component of SECU was crafted by [Vanderbilt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University "Vanderbilt University") Chancellor [Nicholas S. Zeppos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_S._Zeppos "Nicholas S. Zeppos"), who at the time was the Vice President of the SEC Executive Committee and liaison to SECU.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-55) In an interview with Dr. Zeppos about the formation of the SECU he noted, "that the member institutions of the Southeastern Conference are committed to a shared mission of fostering research, scholarship, and achievement. The SEC Symposium represents a platform to connect, collaborate and promote a productive dialogue that will span disciplinary and institutional boundaries and allow us to work together for the betterment of society."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-56)

The SEC Academic Network was created in 2009 in partnership with [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN"). The SEC Academic Network was an online library of institutionally produced videos featuring academic initiatives and stories from all Southeastern Conference institutions. The SEC Academic Network was officially merged into the SECU operation.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Conference#cite_note-57)

The '''2022 NFL draft''' was the [[National Football League]]'s 87th annual [[NFL draft|draft]] and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the [[Caesars Forum]] on the [[Las Vegas Strip]] in [[Paradise, Nevada|Paradise]] next to [[Las Vegas]]. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the [[Las Vegas metropolitan area]] and the state of [[Nevada]].

The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in [[1991 NFL draft|1991]]. Along with the [[1972 NFL draft|1972]] and [[2000 NFL draft|2000]] drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia]] defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since [[2013 NFL draft|2013]]. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since [[1997 NFL draft|1997]], and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since [[2014 NFL draft|2014]].

A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/the-nfl-draft-was-just-another-wild-night-in-vegas-now-which-teams-will-regret-it-044817056.html |title=The NFL draft was just another wild night in Vegas. Now which teams will regret it? |first=Dan |last=Wetzel |website=Yahoo Sports |date=April 29, 2022 |access-date=April 30, 2022}}</ref>

==Host city==
Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the [[2020 NFL draft]], coinciding with the [[Oakland Raiders relocation to Las Vegas|Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city]]. Due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] the draft was held as a [[virtual event]]. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.<ref>{{cite web |title=Las Vegas will play host to 2022 NFL Draft |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/las-vegas-will-play-host-to-2022-nfl-draft-0ap3000001110804|website=NFL.com |access-date=April 23, 2020 |date=April 23, 2020|last=Gordon|first=Grant}}</ref>

Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating [[red carpet]] on the man-made lake in front of the [[Bellagio (resort)|Bellagio]] and its [[Fountains of Bellagio|fountains]]. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=2022 NFL Draft is going full Las Vegas, but will be missing one key detail from the original plan |url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/2022-nfl-draft-is-going-full-las-vegas-but-will-be-missing-one-key-detail-from-the-original-plan/ |access-date=April 28, 2022 |website=CBSSports.com |last=Breech|first=John|date=April 26, 2022}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Horwath |first=Bryan |date=April 28, 2022 |title=Caesars Entertainment ecstatically hosts the 2022 NFL Draft after a prolonged wait |url=https://lasvegassun.com/news/2022/apr/28/caesars-entertainment-hosts-the-2022-nfl-draft/ |access-date=April 28, 2022 |website=Las Vegas Sun }}</ref>

Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> [[The Linq Promenade]] hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Parts of [[Flamingo Road (Las Vegas)|Flamingo Road]] and [[Las Vegas Boulevard]] were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 26, 2022 |title=What to know about traffic around Las Vegas during the NFL Draft |url=https://news3lv.com/news/local/what-to-know-about-traffic-around-las-vegas-during-the-nfl-draft |access-date=April 28, 2022 |website=KSNV|via=News 3 Staff}}</ref>

[[Paradise, Nevada]] | network = [[ESPN]], [[ESPN2]], [[ESPN on ABC|ABC]], [[NFL Network]], [[ESPN Deportes]], [[ESPN Radio]] | sponsor = | league = [[National Football League]] | first = [[Travon Walker]], DE, [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] | mr_irrelevant = [[Brock Purdy]], QB, [[San Francisco 49ers]] | fewnum = 4 | fewest = [[2022 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] | mostnum = 11 | most = {{ubl|[[2022 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]]|[[2022 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]]|[[2022 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]]|[[2022 New York Giants season|New York Giants]]}} | overall = 262 | rounds = 7 | hofnum = | prev = [[2021 NFL draft|2021]] | next = [[2023 NFL draft|2023]] }} The '''2022 NFL draft''' was the [[National Football League]]'s 87th annual [[NFL draft|draft]] and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the [[Caesars Forum]] on the [[Las Vegas Strip]] in [[Paradise, Nevada|Paradise]] next to [[Las Vegas]]. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the [[Las Vegas metropolitan area]] and the state of [[Nevada]]. The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in [[1991 NFL draft|1991]]. Along with the [[1972 NFL draft|1972]] and [[2000 NFL draft|2000]] drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia]] defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since [[2013 NFL draft|2013]]. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since [[1997 NFL draft|1997]], and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since [[2014 NFL draft|2014]]. A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/the-nfl-draft-was-just-another-wild-night-in-vegas-now-which-teams-will-regret-it-044817056.html |title=The NFL draft was just another wild night in Vegas. Now which teams will regret it? |first=Dan |last=Wetzel |website=Yahoo Sports |date=April 29, 2022 |access-date=April 30, 2022}} ==Host city== Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the [[2020 NFL draft]], coinciding with the [[Oakland Raiders relocation to Las Vegas|Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city]]. Due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] the draft was held as a [[virtual event]]. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.{{cite web |title=Las Vegas will play host to 2022 NFL Draft |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/las-vegas-will-play-host-to-2022-nfl-draft-0ap3000001110804|website=NFL.com |access-date=April 23, 2020 |date=April 23, 2020|last=Gordon|first=Grant}} Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating [[red carpet]] on the man-made lake in front of the [[Bellagio (resort)|Bellagio]] and its [[Fountains of Bellagio|fountains]]. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.{{Cite web |title=2022 NFL Draft is going full Las Vegas, but will be missing one key detail from the original plan |url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/2022-nfl-draft-is-going-full-las-vegas-but-will-be-missing-one-key-detail-from-the-original-plan/ |access-date=April 28, 2022 |website=CBSSports.com |last=Breech|first=John|date=April 26, 2022}}{{Cite web |last=Horwath |first=Bryan |date=April 28, 2022 |title=Caesars Entertainment ecstatically hosts the 2022 NFL Draft after a prolonged wait |url=https://lasvegassun.com/news/2022/apr/28/caesars-entertainment-hosts-the-2022-nfl-draft/ |access-date=April 28, 2022 |website=Las Vegas Sun }} Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event. [[The Linq Promenade]] hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities. Parts of [[Flamingo Road (Las Vegas)|Flamingo Road]] and [[Las Vegas Boulevard]] were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.{{Cite web |date=April 26, 2022
